title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
content:
In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape.
Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing “exponential growth” in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels.
The investment in Fujifilm’s Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it “the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities.” The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation “FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10” tape.
Mainstream consumers may have abandoned tape decades ago, but the enterprise world never did. Cloud giants rely on tape to back up vast troves of data. Fujifilm’s work with magnetic tape as a data storage medium dates back to the 1950s, and in 2000, the company released its first LTO Ultrium storage tape. In 2011, the company was the first to commercially produce tape with barium ferrite magnetic particles, and in 2025 it debuted the LTO Ultrium10, the first storage solution in the medium to use what the company calls “fine hybrid magnetic particles” by combining barium ferrite with strontium ferrite tech. Each generation of tape (currently Gen 10) has seen meaningful increases in both compressed and uncompressed storage limits.
According to Fujifilm, “major cloud service and data center operators” have been expanding their use of magnetic tape because it can store large data volumes at relatively low cost. Tape backups can be easily disconnected and stored in a drawer, a vault, or a separate facility. Fujifilm highlights the ability to air-gap tape cartridges as a last defense for user data: “Given the sophistication of cyberattacks, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware.”

report.summary: Fujifilm will invest about $63 million to expand LTO magnetic tape output fivefold by fiscal 2028, citing generative AI-driven data archiving demand.
report.background: Fujifilm has made magnetic tape since the 1950s and released its first LTO Ultrium tape in 2000, so the announcement extends a long enterprise storage business rather than a consumer revival. Consumers moved to disks and cloud, but cloud providers and data centers kept tape for backups and archives because it stores huge volumes at low cost per terabyte. Fujifilm introduced barium ferrite particles in 2011 and debuted LTO Ultrium10 in 2025 using fine hybrid magnetic particles that combine barium ferrite and strontium ferrite. Each LTO generation has raised compressed and uncompressed capacity. The immediate trigger is generative AI: training and inference generate exponential data volumes, while regulations and business continuity require long retention. Tape also offers an air gap that ransomware cannot reach remotely.
key_points: Fujifilm will spend roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to raise LTO tape production capacity fivefold versus fiscal 2025 levels. The project at its Kanagawa Factory's Odawara site runs from fiscal 2026 through 2028, adds manufacturing space and personnel, and is Fujifilm's largest investment yet in dedicated LTO tape facilities, focused mainly on LTO Ultrium10.

Fujifilm says generative AI is creating "exponential growth" in worldwide data needs. Major cloud service and data center operators are expanding tape use because it stores large volumes at relatively low cost, making tape a key archival tier behind AI training data, logs, backups, and long-term records.

Tape never disappeared from enterprise storage. Fujifilm's LTO lineage dates to 2000, and its 2025 LTO Ultrium10 uses fine hybrid magnetic particles combining barium ferrite and strontium ferrite. Each generation has increased compressed and uncompressed capacity, helping tape compete for dense, low-cost archive storage.

Fujifilm is pitching air-gapped cartridges as ransomware defense. Tape can be disconnected and stored in a drawer, vault, or separate facility, so attackers cannot reach it over a network. That security property, plus low cost, is driving renewed interest as cyberattacks become more sophisticated.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the expansion signals that storage, not just GPUs, is becoming a constraint. AI pipelines create massive training sets, checkpoints, logs, and compliance records; cheap tape archives free expensive disk and flash for active workloads. Developers should expect more tiered storage designs and may need tape-aware backup or LTFS workflows for long-term datasets. Regular users are unlikely to buy tape, but they benefit indirectly if cloud providers reduce archiving costs and improve ransomware resilience. The investment also shows AI's physical supply chain: old technologies can become strategic again when data volumes outpace conventional storage economics. It may also influence cloud archive pricing and durability guarantees.
report.tools: Follow the LTO Program roadmap and Fujifilm's LTO Ultrium10 specifications. For hands-on tape workflows, LTFS (Linear Tape File System) presents tapes as a filesystem; open-source backup suites with tape support include Bacula, Bareos, and Amanda. These are useful for evaluating archive automation, media rotation, and air-gapped backups without proprietary lock-in.
